title: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2
assumption: Adding 1 to a number and adding 2 to the same number always give different results.

input.description: An auto-incrementing counter, row id, or 'view count' stored as a plain JS number that has climbed past 2^53.

what_goes_wrong: A counter that increments a plain JS `number` past 2^53 - 1 stops being able to tell consecutive values apart: incrementing by 1 does nothing some of the time, so a counter can appear to stall or two different logical events can be recorded with the identical numeric id.
why: JS numbers are IEEE 754 double-precision floats, which have 53 bits of mantissa and so they represent every integer exactly only up to 2^53. `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` is 2^53 - 1 because it is the largest n for which n and n + 1 are both exact. Between 2^53 and 2^54 the representable doubles are 2 apart, so `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1` is exactly 2^53, and `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2` (2^53 + 1) sits halfway between 2^53 and 2^53 + 2 and rounds, ties-to-even, down to 2^53 as well.

repros.code:
# Python ints are arbitrary precision, so the same arithmetic never collides.
max_safe = 2**53 - 1
print(max_safe + 1 == max_safe + 2)
print(max_safe + 1, max_safe + 2)

fix: Use `BigInt` (or a string) for any counter, id, or accumulated value that could exceed 2^53 - 1 in JavaScript; check `Number.isSafeInteger()` before trusting equality/ordering on a large computed number.

test_cases.note: A safe-integer check should flag this value's successor as unsafe, not silently accept it.
